newsitem.title: ESTONIA: Estonia pursues reform despite political turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Estonia pursues reform despite political turmoil.

text.p: The small Baltic state of Estonia, hit by fresh political crisis, has managed to pursue economic reforms despite political turmoil to become one of eastern Europe's success stories, analysts said.
Prime Minister Tiit Vaehi announced on Wednesday that he plans to resign after a humiliatingly close no-confidence vote on Monday, which he only narrowly won.
Vaehi is leading Estonia's sixth government since the country split from the former Soviet Union in 1991.

"The main reason for the economic success is the broad consensus for reform which has been maintained despite changes in the government," Dimitri Demekas, Estonia's International Monetary Fund (IMF) resident representative, told Reuters.
With a population of just 1.5 million, Estonia was scorned as an insignificant minnow when it split from Moscow along with its Baltic cousins Latvia and Lithuania.
Many analysts expected it to continue strong links with Moscow, to which it had long been tied under the centrally-planned Soviet system.
But the country has gained many admirers in the region for pursuing fast-track privatisation of its state-owned companies and having an open, Western-oriented economy.

"Despite the various governments there has been a consistent policy from those at the top to follow similar economic policies," Ardo Hansson, Vaehi's economic advisor and central bank board member, told Reuters.
Analysts say that some 60 percent of economic activity is in the private sector while for services it is nearer 90 percent.
The influential Washington Post recently held Estonia up as an example for huge neighbour Russia to follow.
After inflation soared to more than 1,000 percent in the wake of its regaining of independence, Estonia's prices last year rose by 14.8 percent.
Economic growth is expected to be around four to five percent in 1997-1998.
It has also attracted a high share of foreign direct investment and gleaming new multi-storey bank buildings are slowly beginning to emerge in the capital, Tallinn.
The kroon currency is also strongly backed and a balanced budget has been enshrined in law.
"Estonia is doing very well, growth is expected to continue and although inflation is high, it will continue to fall," the IMF's Demekas said.
But experts say that economic success may lead to Estonia's small economy overheating and that it faces other problems.
"Estonia is now facing a second wave of reforms much like advanced economies and has to deal with issues like pension reform and controlling municipal borrowing," Demekas said.
